description_full: Northland Power Inc. operates as a power producer in Canada, the Netherlands, Germany, Colombia, Spain, the United States, and internationally. The company produces electricity from renewable resources, such as offshore and onshore wind; solar; natural gas; and battery energy storage for sale under power purchase agreements and other revenue arrangements. As of December 31, 2025, it owned or had a net economic interest in 3,014 MW of power-producing facilities with a total gross operating capacity of approximately 3,498 MW and a regulated utility. The company was founded in 1987 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada.
ceo_bio: Ms. Christine M. Healy | President, CEO & Director | Age 53 | Compensation: $2.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $1.5M ranks in the top quartile among Utilities peers. Each employee generates $795K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10). R&D investment of 3% of revenue (limited) signals commitment to product development and talent.
financial_summary: Northland Power, Inc. is a mid-cap utilities business with a $4.3B market cap on $1.7B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are contracting by -3.3pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 5% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 90% confirm genuine pricing power.
The business throws off $906M in free cash flow — roughly 53 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

news_headlines.title: Northland Power (OTCMKTS:NPIFF) Shares Gap Up on Strong Earnings

sect: Its 32% operating margin runs 11pp above the Utilities median (21%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.68x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 97 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 31% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 8% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.62, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.02 vs 5y 0.51), so read it loosely.
About $1.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 24% in the 2022 bear market and 43% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 71% below its DCF fair value of $57.42, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $9.78 to $200 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Utilities peers: P/E 13.3 vs 19.5, EV/EBITDA 7.0 vs 12.5 and P/FCF 4.8 vs 19.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 20.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 13.0% annual cash-flow growth, 12pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 6% earns above the cost of capital of 5.4%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.22).
It runs a 90% gross margin and converts 53% of revenue into free cash flow.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.1x net debt to EBITDA ($451.6M of cash against $4.8B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.5x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.63 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.5% over 3 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 41%.
It returns 4.6% a year to shareholders (3.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years.
people: With about 1,139 employees, each generates about $1.5M of revenue, 1.5x the Utilities median.
That works out to $795K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.6M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
